projects.title: Turbo Gauge
projects.summary: A DIY OBD-II boost + IAT + Oil Temp gauge for a 2025 Acura Integra. Custom dual round displays, built to my specs instead of buying an expensive unit that still doesn’t fit what I want.
projects.why: There aren't any decent gauges for my car with the specs I wanted. And the options that came close were all very expensive. I decided to build one to my own specs. This alows be to make it cheaper, have a dual-display layout which is what I actually want, and a car-safe OBD path that doesn’t require splicing factory sensors.
projects.what: A work-in-progress DIY boost gauge for a 2025 Acura Integra. The plan is read-only OBD-II / CAN data into an ESP32, shown on two round TFTs: a larger 2.1" GC9B72 (360×360) for boost and a smaller 1.28" GC9A01 (240×240) for IAT, and old temp. Power is intended from a fused 12V tap through a buck converter. No vacuum taps, no ECU harness splicing: unplug the OBD cable and the car is stock again.
projects.challenges: Getting the round-display UI to look clean on real panels took several passes. Early gauge drawing looked uneven until the faces were rebuilt. Display drivers and brightness matching between the two screens mattered on the bench. On the car side, the hard constraint is staying read-only and not turning this into anything that writes the bus or splices sensors. Power and wiring are denser than a breadboard toy: shared SPI lines, 5V vs 3.3V levels, fuse-tap strategy, and a cable plan that can later reach from OBD/CAN to a dash pod without making a mess. Confirming which PIDs the 2025 Integra actually exposes still has to be proven on the car.
projects.outcome: Still in progress. What’s working now is the visual direction on a simulator plus bench hardware bringing up the dual round displays and iterating the UI. What’s next is closing the loop with real OBD/CAN data, then packaging power, cabling, and a printed mount so it’s usable in the Integra, without assuming the final form until those pieces land.

projects.title: Fog Collector Door Mechanism
projects.summary: A motorized door that opens for fog collection and closes to keep dust and debris out of remote fog collectors near farms and open terrain.
projects.why: Fog collectors are often installed in remote sites. For example, in one location, tractors regularly kicked up heavy dust that could contaminate the system. We needed a door that stays closed when collection is not needed, keeping unwanted particulates out, and opens whenever fog is present so the collector can do its job.
projects.what: A redesigned door mechanism for outdoor fog collectors. The system moves solid polycarbonate doors with a drivetrain intended for reliable open/close cycles in dusty and remote conditions, sealed when it is not.
projects.how: The design moved from a four-motor layout to a single-motor chain-driven drivetrain to cut cost, complexity, and reliability (about 25% fewer components and door closes better). I CAD'd the mechanism, 3D printed a 20% scale prototype to validate motion, and developed the full-scale outdoor version. Upcoming work includes integrating motors, wiring, and control so the door can open and close on a schedule or condition trigger.
projects.challenges: Sizing torque for solid polycarbonate doors is a core constraint: enough force to move the panels reliably outdoors without overbuilding the drivetrain. Other challenges include keeping the mechanism tolerant of dust and weather, designing a door design that will open all the way not blocking the flow of the fog into the collector, choosing materials and fasteners that hold up outside, and leaving room for motors and wiring so electrical integration does not fight the mechanical layout later.
projects.outcome: Still in progress. Mechanical design and hands-on fabrication are underway; motor integration and field-ready actuation are next. More photos, build notes, and results will be added as the project continues.

projects.title: Sentinel AI
projects.summary: A 24-hour NVIDIA hackathon build: a multi-agentic system that simulates, detects, and investigates cloud security breaches.
projects.why: Cloud breaches on platforms like AWS are expensive due to downtime, data exposure, incident response, and compliance fallout can cost companies millions. After hearing about recurring cloud security failures, our team wanted a system that does more than raise an alert: something that can simulate threats, catch suspicious activity, and dig into incidents the way a security analyst would, but faster and with coordinated AI agents.
projects.what: Sentinel AI is a multi-agentic security workflow. It can simulate cloud breach scenarios, detect anomalous or malicious patterns, and then autonomously investigate, gathering context, correlating signals, and producing a structured incident narrative so responders see what happened and why, not just a raw alarm.
projects.how: We architected six specialized LLM agents, each with a focused job in the pipeline (for example: simulation, detection, investigation, and reporting), so no single model had to do everything. The agents ran on NVIDIA Nemotron models via OpenRouter and were coordinated through the OpenClaw agent framework, handing off findings between stages so detection output fed investigation, and investigation fed a clearer final summary.
projects.challenges: Twenty-four hours forced ruthless scope control: which agents were essential, what to stub, and what to demo live. Coordinating six agents without messy loops or contradictory conclusions was hard: prompts, handoffs, and failure cases all had to stay stable under time pressure. Tooling and API limits also bit: keeping OpenRouter/Nemotron calls reliable while we iterated the architecture meant debugging orchestration and agent boundaries as much as the security logic itself.
projects.outcome: We shipped a working end-to-end demo within the 24-hour NVIDIA hackathon: simulation → detection → autonomous investigation across the six-agent system. Next improvements would be deeper AWS-specific telemetry, stronger evaluation of false positives, and a cleaner operator UI for real incident response workflows.

projects.title: Pan-Tilt Tracking Turret
projects.summary: A vision-guided pan/tilt turret that tracks a target with YOLO + a Kalman filter, then PID-drives steppers from a Teensy so a laser stays on the target.

videos.title: Final build: tracking a hand in real time
V1 turret first prototype / motion demo

projects.why: I wanted computer vision to do something physical, not just draw boxes on a screen. This project closes that loop: detect a target, drive a pan/tilt mount in real time, and keep a laser on it while the target moves.
projects.what: A vision-guided pan/tilt turret. A Mac runs Ultralytics YOLO and a 2D Kalman filter on a live camera feed, sends pixel error over USB serial to a Teensy 4.1, and the Teensy PID-controls NEMA steppers through STEPPERONLINE CL42T closed-loop drivers. A laser on the mount shows aim. Modes (idle / track / manual) and live pan/tilt PID gains are controlled from a local Flask UI, with a belt-driven tilt axis and a 3D-printed structure carrying the camera payload.
projects.how: Each frame is downscaled for inference. YOLO picks the largest detection above a size threshold (default nano.pt; hand.pt for the hand-tracking demo). A 2D Kalman filter smooths the box center and predicts through short misses, then pixel error vs. frame center (err_x, err_y) is sent to the Teensy as TARGET:err_x,err_y over USB serial at 115200 baud. On the Teensy, AccelStepper drives pan (STEP/DIR on pins 2/3) and tilt (4/5) in error mode: separate pan/tilt PID loops map pixel error into commanded RPM, with integral clamping and direction signs. SET_GAINS and SET_VELOCITY commands let the Flask UI retune Kp/Ki/Kd live and push manual velocity; gains persist to saved_data/gains.json. Idle stops motion; track is the closed loop; manual bypasses vision and drives velocity from the UI.
projects.challenges: Closing the loop meant fighting lag and oscillation at the same time: too much PID gain and the turret hunts; too little and it loses the target. Deadbands on pixel error, Kalman process/measurement noise, max-missed prediction, and max jump limits all had to be tuned so short detection dropouts did not yank the motors. Serial timing and Teensy PID dt handling mattered. Bad dt spikes would spike the derivative term. Mechanically, belt-driven tilt, closed-loop steppers, and a printed structure had to stay stiff enough that the laser aim matched what vision thought was center. On the host side, inference speed (MPS vs CPU), confidence/min-area thresholds, and “largest box wins” tracking all affected whether the laser followed the intended target or something louder in the frame.
projects.outcome: Shipped a working end-to-end demo: live camera → YOLO → Kalman → serial error → Teensy PID → pan/tilt steppers with a laser on target, including a hand-tracking demo and an earlier V1 motion prototype. Host and firmware live in the Auto-Tracking-Turret repo. Next improvements would be returning to a true center pose in idle (instead of only stopping motors), stronger multi-target selection, and cleaner packaging of the wiring and enclosure for demos.
